ComprehensionText:
from Confetti Girl by Diana López

1 Mom always had after-school projects waiting for me. "Can you help decorate cookies?" she'd say. Or, "Go outside and pick some flowers." Or, "Fix my nails, please." She loved to paint them, but since she wasn't coordinated with her left hand, her right-hand nails looked like a preschooler's coloring page.

2 I guess these projects were chores, but they were fun, too. Now when I come home, I've got to sweep, fold towels, or scrub the bathroom sink. Dad helps, but sometimes he makes a big mess.

3 Like today. He's got flour, potato skins, and crumpled napkins on the counter. The pot boils over with brown scum. And I don't want to talk to him because I'm still mad about the volleyball game, but I have to know what he's up to.

4 "What are you doing, Dad?"

5 "Making dinner. Thought I'd give you a break."

6 Except for game nights, dinner's my responsibility. I cook while Dad cleans—that's our rule. And even though I don't cook as well as Mom did, Dad never complains.

7 "What are you going to make?" I ask.

8 "Carne guisada and papas fritas."

9 "You need a recipe for that?"

10 "Are you kidding? I need a recipe for peanut butter sandwiches."

11 How mad can a girl be at a man who makes fun of himself and wears a green frog apron that says KISS THE COOK and tube socks over his hands for potholders?

5 Grade 8 English Language Arts—Session 1

12 We clear space on the table. Dinner's served. The beef's tough and the papas are mushy, but who cares? I pretend it's delicious because my dad lets me blabber about the Halloween carnival. He laughs out loud when I describe Vanessa's potato baby and Ms. Cantu's creative cascarones, ^1 so I don't complain when I notice he served ranch‐style beans straight from the can instead of heating them up first.

13 Everything's great until he asks about my English class.

14 "Any new vocabulary words?" he wants to know.

15 "I guess. Maybe. Super . . . super . . . super something. Can't remember."

16 "Was it supersede?" he asks. "Supercilious? Superfluous?"

17 "I don't remember, Dad. It could have been super-duper or super-loop for all I care."

18 He gets sarcasm from his students all the time so he's good at ignoring it.

19 "Remember that super is a prefix that means 'above and beyond,' " he says. "So no matter what the word is, you can get its meaning if you take it apart."

20 "Okay, Dad. I get it. So did I tell you we're having a book sale for our next fundraiser?"

21 "What else are you doing in English?" he asks. "Reading any novels?"

22 I sigh, bored, but he doesn't get the hint. He just waits for my answer. "Yes," I finally say. "I don't remember the title, but it's got a rabbit on the cover."

23 "Is it Watership Down? It's got to be Watership Down."

24 "Yes, that's it. But I left it in my locker. I guess I can't do my homework."

25 "Nonsense. I've got a copy somewhere. Let me look."

26 He leaves the table to scan the bookshelves, and all of the sudden, I care about the tough beef, the mushy potatoes, and the cold beans. Why should I eat when my own father has abandoned his food? Nothing's more important than his books and vocabulary words. He might say I matter, but when he goes on a scavenger hunt for a book, I realize that I really don't.

27 I take my plate to the kitchen, grab my half-finished soda, and head to my room. When I walk past him, he's kneeling to search the lower shelves. He's got a paper towel and wipes it lovingly over the titles as if polishing a sports car. He doesn't hear my angry, stomping footsteps. I catch the last part of his sentence. cascarones—hollow eggs filled with confetti or toys 1 Grade 8 6 English Language Arts—Session 1

28 ". . . a classic epic journey," he says as if he were in class with a bunch of students. I can't stand it. I just can't stand it. I'd rather have Vanessa's crazy mom.

29 Later, just as I write I love Luís for the three-hundredth time, my dad peeks through my bedroom door.

30 "Found my copy of Watership Down," he says, handing me a paperback whose spine's been taped a dozen times. "How far do you have to read tonight?"

31 "The first four chapters," I say.

32 "That's a lot. You better get busy."

33 "Sure, Dad. I'll start reading right away."

34 But I don't. As soon as he leaves, I put the book on my nightstand and use it as a coaster. The condensation from my soda makes a big, wet circle on the cover. From CONFETTI GIRL by Diana López. Copyright © 2009 by Diana López. By permission of Little, Brown, and Company.

from Tortilla Sun by Jennifer Cervantes

1 Clang cla-clang, clang clang. The next morning, I found Mom in the kitchen with a chisel and hammer, chipping away at the kitchen counter. Little flecks of white flew through the air like ceramic snow, landing softly on her olive-colored cheeks.

2 I ducked as a piece of tile flew at me. "Hey!"

3 She turned toward me with a look of surprise. "Morning, Izzy. I didn't see you standing there."

4 "Wha . . . what are you doing?" I asked.

5 She stepped back and surveyed the half-demolished counter the way someone stands back to study a newly hung photograph. Wiping her cheek with the back of her hand she said, "There was this"—she searched the mess on the floor—"this one broken tile poking out and I thought I should fix it and . . ."

6 I pushed past her to get the broom but she grabbed me by the elbow. A feeling of nervousness swelled inside me.

7 "Izzy, wait. I have something to tell you."

8 There it was. My heart buckled in my chest. Something was wrong.

9 Mom leaned back against the counter and sucked in a great gulp of air. "It's strange actually. I wasn't expecting it, but then at the last minute the funding came through." She folded her arms across her waist. "I'm going to Costa Rica to finish my research."

10 Her words buzzed around me like a swarm of confused bees. "When? For how long?"

11 "I'll be gone for most of the summer. I leave Tuesday."

12 Mom wouldn't leave me. We'd go together. Right? "But that's only three days away." I stepped away from Mom and the shards of tile.

13 "I don't have a choice."

14 "But what am I supposed to do? That's three whole months."

15 "Two. I'll be home at the end of July. And after this I can finally graduate. Our lives will change then." She reached over and stroked my hair. "For the better." Grade 8 10 English Language Arts—Session 1

16 I rolled those three words around in my mind: for the better.

17 Suddenly last night's phone call made perfect sense. I inched closer and pushed at the broken tile with my toes.

18 "Are you sending me to Nana's?" I asked. "In New Mexico?"

19 A flash of surprise crossed Mom's face. Like she knew I had heard her phone conversation. "She's so excited to have you and . . ."

20 "What happened to all your talk about you guys not seeing eye to eye?" I asked.

21 "It's not that we don't see eye to eye. We just don't see the world the same way."

22 "Why can't I go with you?" I said.

23 "Izzy . . ."

24 "New Mexico is worlds away from California. And what am I going to do for two whole months with someone I haven't seen since I was six? That was half my life ago. She's a stranger!" I felt a sudden urge to bolt for the front door and run.

25 Mom rolled her eyes. "Oh, Izzy. She's hardly a stranger. She's family. I already have your ticket. You leave Monday." Mom opened the refrigerator and took out a diet soda, pressing the cold can against her face before opening it.

26 I stared at the mess on the floor. "Why can't I stay here? Alone." My voice quivered.

27 Mom took a swig of her soda, then closed her eyes and took a deep breath. When she opened them, she spoke slowly and deliberately.

28 "You're going to New Mexico and that's final."

29 I swallowed hard and tried not to cry. "Why do you always get to decide everything? We just unpacked and I—I had plans."

30 She raised her eyebrows, surprised. "Plans?"

31 Mom was always bugging me to make friends, which I didn't see the point of, considering we moved every few months. And we moved for all sorts of reasons: closer to the university for her, better school for me, quieter, prettier, bigger, smaller.

32 "I was going to try and find some girls my age here in the complex so I wouldn't have to be the new kid in school again," I said, trying to sound believable.

33 "Honey, you can make friends at your new school in the fall. Besides, this is a wonderful opportunity for you."

11 Grade 8 English Language Arts—Session 1

34 "Opportunity? For me? Or for you?"

35 I stormed off to my room and threw myself onto my bed. I ached inside. Like the feeling you get watching a lost balloon float far into the sky until it becomes an invisible nothing.

36 I reached for a story card and scribbled:

37 Gypsy was sent to prison for stealing the magic ball. And when she was tossed into the dungeon below the castle she found the word "opportunity" written across the stone wall.

38 Staring at the card, I wondered what should happen next. Maybe a daring escape or a sorceress could rescue her. When nothing came to me, I scratched out the word opportunity until it was a big blob of blue ink and tossed the card on the floor.

39 I heard Mom's footsteps coming toward my closed bedroom door. I held my breath, hoping she wouldn't knock.

40 Tap. Tap.

41 Silence.

42 "Izzy?" she spoke quietly.

43 My hands wandered beneath my pillow and gripped the baseball I had hidden there. I squeezed my eyes closed and whispered, "I wish I didn't have to go. I wish I didn't have to go."

44 "I've brought your suitcase." She stood outside my door for what seemed like forever. I pictured her on the other side, arms crossed, head down.

45 "I think you're going to like the village." Her voice became a little muffled now, like her mouth was pressed right up against the door. "It's strange and beautiful at the same time and a perfect place to explore. You just might be surprised what you find there." She paused for a moment then continued. "Would you please talk to me?"

46 I burrowed my head under the pillow with the baseball. A tiny piece of me felt guilty for stealing it, but it belonged to my dad and that made it special. That made it a part of me.

47 "I'll just leave the suitcase here for you," she said. Her bare feet slapped against the tile and carried her away.

QuestionText: The passage from Confetti Girl begins with the narrator's memories of her mother (paragraph 1). The passage from Tortilla Sun ends with Izzy's thoughts about the baseball that belonged to her father (paragraph 46). How do these paragraphs contribute to an understanding of both narrators?
AnswerA: The paragraphs reveal that the narrators have little reason to feel upset about their present situations.
AnswerB: The paragraphs suggest the efforts the narrators will go to so that they may please their parents.
AnswerC: The paragraphs emphasize the fact that the narrators may not be reporting events truthfully.
AnswerD: The paragraphs highlight the narrators' strong desire to regain a sense of closeness.

ComprehensionText:
Treasure from the Roadside
Most artists build their careers in their twenties and thirties. Rosalie Gascoigne held her first solo exhibition at the age of fifty-seven, using materials that most people would have driven straight past: weathered road signs, broken soft-drink crates, rusty iron and the feathers of swans. Within a few years, she was one of the most admired artists in Australia.
Gascoigne was born in Auckland, New Zealand, in 1917. In 1943 she married an astronomer, Ben Gascoigne, and moved with him to Mount Stromlo Observatory, on a hilltop outside Canberra. It was a lonely place for a young mother. The observatory was isolated, the community was small, and the dry, windswept paddocks looked nothing like the green hills of her childhood. For years she felt like a stranger in the landscape.
Her way of coming to terms with it was to walk. While her husband studied the stars, she explored the grasslands of the Monaro and the roadsides around Canberra, bringing home things that caught her eye: smooth stones, sheep bones, dried thistles, sheets of rusted corrugated iron. She began arranging them, at first simply to decorate the house. In the 1960s she studied ikebana, the Japanese art of flower arranging, which taught her to think carefully about line, space and balance.
Gradually her arrangements became something more. She started to create assemblages, works made by combining found objects. She never painted the landscape directly. Instead she tried to capture how it felt: the glare of the light on dry grass, the rhythm of fence posts, the way a paddock looks from a moving car. In one well-known work, she pushed hundreds of swan feathers into a wire fence frame, so that it seemed to shimmer like a flock in flight.
Her most famous works used old road signs. Gascoigne collected them from tips and roadsides, cut them into strips and squares, then rearranged the pieces in grids. Letters were broken up so the words no longer made sense, and what remained were patterns of bright yellow, black and white. Viewers often say these works suggest sunlight flickering across fields or the endless repetition of a country road.
Recognition came quickly once it began. Galleries bought her work, and in 1982 she was chosen to represent Australia at the Venice Biennale, one of the world's most important art events. Yet she never stopped scavenging. Friends remembered her roaming the tips with a sharp eye, delighted by a faded plank or a sun-bleached sign that nobody else wanted.
Gascoigne died in 1999, but her work remains in major galleries across Australia. Her story is often told as one of a late beginning, and it is that. It is also a story about looking. She spent decades in a landscape that at first seemed empty and harsh to her, and by paying close attention to it, and to the things others had thrown away, she found beauty that had been there all along.

ComprehensionText:
Nobody Invited Them
In August 1947, a grand new arts festival opened in Edinburgh, Scotland. Its organisers had invited orchestras, opera companies and famous theatre groups from across Europe. But eight small theatre companies that had not been invited turned up anyway. Rather than going home, they found whatever spaces they could and put on their shows around the edges of the official program. A local writer described their efforts as happening on the 'fringe' of the festival, and the name stuck.
Those uninvited performers started something remarkable. Today, the Edinburgh Festival Fringe is one of the largest arts festivals on the planet, with thousands of shows each August staged in theatres, school halls, cafes, lecture rooms and even a double-decker bus. Its central rule is simple: there is no selection panel. If you can find a venue and pay the registration fee, you can perform.
Australia has embraced the idea. The Adelaide Fringe began in 1960 and is now the largest arts festival in the Southern Hemisphere. During February and March, the city is transformed. Comedians perform in shipping containers, jugglers fill the parks, and a magician might share a laneway with a string quartet.
I believe the open-door model is the best way to run a festival, and our school's annual arts night should adopt it.
At the moment, a committee of teachers chooses which acts will perform. The committee does a careful job, but the result is predictable. The same confident students, usually those who already take music or drama lessons, appear every year. Plenty of talented people never audition because they assume they will not be picked.
A fringe removes that barrier. Without a panel deciding who is good enough, performers take risks. Some shows will be brilliant, some will be odd and a few may fall flat. That is part of the fun. Edinburgh has launched the careers of countless comedians, writers and actors who were unknown when they first arrived. Nobody would have chosen them in advance, but audiences discovered them.
An open festival also builds its audience in a different way. At a fringe, people do not simply sit through one long program. They wander from show to show, take a chance on something unfamiliar and tell their friends what they found. Imagine our school grounds with a poetry reading in the library, a band on the basketball court and a science magic show in Lab 3, all running at once.
Critics may worry that some acts will not be polished. They are right; some will not. But a festival is not an exam. Its purpose is to celebrate creativity, and creativity is often messy before it is marvellous. The organisers can still set sensible rules about safety, time limits and suitable content without judging talent.
In 1947, eight groups refused to wait for an invitation. Our school does not have to make its performers wait either. Let's open the doors, hand out a map of venues and see who turns up.

AnswerA: They had been chosen by the festival's organisers.
AnswerB: They were too nervous to perform in large theatres.
AnswerC: They were determined to perform without an invitation.
AnswerD: They came to Edinburgh only to watch the orchestras.

ComprehensionText:
The Toll of Merrow Bridge
In the valley town of Merrow, the only way across the river was an old stone bridge, and under the bridge lived a troll whose name nobody knew. Nobody had ever asked.
The troll was not cruel, but he was particular. Every traveller who wished to cross had to pay a toll, and the toll was always the same: 'Give me something you have never given anyone before.'
The merchants of Merrow thought this a fine bargain. The goldsmith handed over a ring he had made that very morning. The weaver gave a scarf woven from thread so fine it floated. The mayor, who liked to make an impression, offered a silver cup polished until it shone like the moon. The troll accepted each gift with a heavy nod and stepped aside.
Yet the troll grew no happier. If anything, he grew greyer and more hunched each season, and his treasures piled up in a damp, gleaming heap that he never looked at. Stranger still, the bridge began to crack. Fine lines crept across the stones, then wider ones. The townsfolk muttered that the troll's sour mood was seeping into the bridge itself, for everyone knew that a troll and his bridge share one heart.
'Pay him more,' said the mayor. 'Something truly magnificent.' So the town collected its finest treasures, and still the cracks grew.
One spring morning, a girl named Edda arrived at the bridge with a basket of eggs to sell at the market on the far side. She was the stonemason's youngest apprentice, and she had nothing of value: no rings, no silver, not even a coin.
'Give me something you have never given anyone before,' rumbled the troll.
Edda thought hard. She looked at the eggs, but she had sold eggs a hundred times. She looked at her hands, rough from carrying stone. Then she looked at the troll himself, really looked, at his drooping ears and the moss growing in the creases of his elbows.
'I have never asked anyone their name,' she said, 'because I already know every name in Merrow. But I don't know yours.'
The troll blinked. For a long moment, the only sound was the river.
'Ormund,' he said at last, in a voice like a small stone rolling. 'My name is Ormund.'
'Good morning, Ormund,' said Edda, and she sat down on the bank beside him. She stayed until the market had closed, asking about the river, the fish and the hundred winters he had spent under the arches. She never did sell her eggs. When she finally stood to leave, she noticed that one of the deepest cracks in the bridge had begun to close, like a wound healing over.
Edda came back the next day, and the day after that, bringing her trowel and a bucket of mortar. As they talked, she patched the smaller cracks, and the larger ones mended on their own.
The goldsmith, watching from his window, could not understand it. 'She paid him nothing,' he complained.
The mayor said nothing at all. But the following week, he walked down to the bridge without his silver cup, stood a little awkwardly in front of the troll, and asked him how he was.

AnswerA: a scarf of very fine thread
AnswerB: a cup polished like the moon
AnswerC: a ring he had made that morning
AnswerD: a basket of fresh eggs

ComprehensionText:
Bringing the Whole Clan Together: How to Plan a Family Reunion
Families today are often scattered across suburbs, states and even continents. Cousins may know each other only through photos, and the stories older relatives carry can fade without anyone noticing. A family reunion gathers everyone in one place, but a good one does not happen by accident. The following steps will help you plan a day that people remember for the right reasons.
Step 1: Form a small team. Planning a reunion alone is exhausting. Ask two or three relatives from different branches of the family to help. A mix of ages works best: an older relative will know who should be invited, while a younger one may be quicker at setting up a group chat or an online invitation.
Step 2: Build the guest list. Start with the oldest living generation and work downwards, branch by branch. It is easy to forget second cousins, new partners or relatives who have moved overseas, so ask each branch to check its own section. A shared spreadsheet with names, contact details and ages will save confusion later.
Step 3: Choose a date and place. Give people at least six months' notice, especially if some must travel long distances. School holidays or long weekends usually suit the most people. When choosing a venue, think about who is coming. A park with shelter, toilets and wheelchair access may suit a crowd of toddlers and elderly relatives better than a restaurant, and it is usually cheaper.
Step 4: Share the costs and the food. A 'bring a plate' lunch spreads the work and lets each household contribute a dish it is proud of. If you need to hire a venue or buy supplies, divide the cost fairly and be open about where the money goes. Arguments about money can sour a reunion before it even begins.
Step 5: Plan activities for every generation. Not everyone will want to sit and chat all day. Organise games that mix ages, such as a trivia quiz about family history with teams that include a grandparent, a parent and a child. A 'memory wall' also works well: invite people to pin up old photographs and label who is in them. Some of the best conversations start when a teenager points at a faded picture and asks, 'Who is that?'
Step 6: Record the day. Ask someone to take photos, and consider setting up a quiet corner where older relatives can be recorded telling stories about their childhood. These recordings often become the most treasured part of the reunion, especially in years to come.
Step 7: Follow up. Within a week, send everyone the photos and a thank-you message. Update the guest list with any new contacts. Then ask the big question: when shall we do it again?
A reunion takes effort, but the reward is more than a pleasant afternoon. When three or four generations share a meal and a laugh, children discover that they belong to a story much larger than themselves.

AnswerD: at least six weeks

Step 2: Build the guest list. Start with the oldest living generation and work downwards, branch by branch. It is easy to forget second cousins, new partners or relatives who have moved overseas, so ask each branch to check its own section. A shared spreadsheet with names, contact details and ages will save confusion later.
Step 3: Choose a date and place. Give people at least six months' notice, especially if some must travel long distances. School holidays or long weekends usually suit the most people. When choosing a venue, think about who is coming. A park with shelter, toilets and wheelchair access may suit a crowd of toddlers and elderly relatives better than a restaurant, and it is usually cheaper.
Step 4: Share the costs and the food. A 'bring a plate' lunch spreads the work and lets each household contribute a dish it is proud of. If you need to hire a venue or buy supplies, divide the cost fairly and be open about where the money goes. Arguments about money can sour a reunion before it even begins.
Step 5: Plan activities for every generation. Not everyone will want to sit and chat all day. Organise games that mix ages, such as a trivia quiz about family history with teams that include a grandparent, a parent and a child. A 'memory wall' also works well: invite people to pin up old photographs and label who is in them. Some of the best conversations start when a teenager points at a faded picture and asks, 'Who is that?'
Step 6: Record the day. Ask someone to take photos, and consider setting up a quiet corner where older relatives can be recorded telling stories about their childhood. These recordings often become the most treasured part of the reunion, especially in years to come.
Step 7: Follow up. Within a week, send everyone the photos and a thank-you message. Update the guest list with any new contacts. Then ask the big question: when shall we do it again?
A reunion takes effort, but the reward is more than a pleasant afternoon. When three or four generations share a meal and a laugh, children discover that they belong to a story much larger than themselves.

Ahmose Writes Home
This is an imagined letter from a boy training to be a scribe in ancient Egypt, about 3300 years ago.
To my father Senu, at the farm beside the eastern canal, from your son Ahmose, at the scribes' school in Thebes. I hope this finds you well and the fields green.
Father, I have received your message. You say the river rose well this year, that the barley stands thick, and that you want me home for the harvest and home for good after it. I have read your words many times, and now I ask you to read mine.
First, let me tell you how my days pass. We rise early and sit in rows in the courtyard, cross-legged, with our writing boards on our knees. Our teacher, old Paneb, reads a line aloud and we copy it. We do not write on papyrus yet, because papyrus is costly and our mistakes are many. Instead we write on flat chips of limestone and broken pieces of pottery, which are everywhere and cost nothing. When a chip is full, we throw it on the pile behind the wall. That pile is now taller than I am, and I think half of it is mine.
My hand has grown steadier. I mix my own ink now: black from soot, red from ochre, each pressed into a little cake and wetted with water. I chew the end of my reed until it frays into a fine brush. Paneb says my signs are beginning to look like signs and less like ants that have fallen into the ink. From Paneb, who has never praised anyone, this is high praise.
Some days we copy lists: the names of birds, of fish, of towns along the river. Other days we copy old letters and wise sayings, so that we learn good manners as well as good signs. The script we use for everyday writing is quicker than the careful pictures carved on temple walls. Paneb says no granary clerk has time to draw a whole owl for every word.
Now, Father, consider what a scribe can do. A scribe counts the grain in the granaries. A scribe measures the fields after the flood washes away the boundary marks, so that every farmer receives his rightful land. A scribe writes the letters that carry news up and down the river. Who measured our own fields last season? A scribe. Who wrote down how much grain we owed? A scribe. If one of our family could do these things, would anyone ever cheat us again?
I know the harvest is hard and the days are long. I have not forgotten the heat, the dust, the ache in my back after a day with the sickle. I am not running from the work, Father. I am learning a different kind of work, one that can protect the work you do.
Paneb says that if I keep at my lessons for four more years, I may be given a place in the office of the granary. Four years is a long time. But a sycamore is not grown in a single season, and you have told me so yourself.
I will come home for the harvest, as you ask, and I will swing a sickle beside my brothers. But when the barley is in, let me return to my chips of stone and my fraying reed. Send your answer with the boatman who brings this letter.
Your son, who still smells of soot,
Ahmose

AnswerC: chips of limestone and broken pottery
AnswerD: flat tablets of dried river clay
